posters.title: Five Agreements for communication
posters.alt: Five classroom agreement adaptations with illustrations of careful words, self-worth, checking assumptions, practice and listening.
text: Classroom adaptations, not rules about what to believe.
1. Use words with care. Be honest. Avoid insults. Repair harm.
2. Remember your worth. Other people’s words do not define you.
3. Check your assumptions. Ask before deciding what someone meant.
4. Practise, don’t seek perfection. Your best can change. Rest and support matter.
5. Question and listen. Check your interpretation. Listen to understand.
Hurtful behaviour is not okay. You can say stop and get help.
Inspired by The Four Agreements by don Miguel Ruiz and The Fifth Agreement by don Miguel Ruiz and don Jose Ruiz.

posters.title: Feelings and shared human needs
posters.alt: Feelings and shared human needs illustrated separately, with examples of different strategies and the distinction between a need and a demand.
text: Different feelings. Needs we all share.
Feelings are clues: calm, excited, worried, frustrated, lonely, curious.
Needs are what matter to us: safety and respect; connection and belonging; rest and care; choice and space; learning and meaning; play and joy.
Same need, different ways: We can both need belonging and choose different activities.
A need is not a demand: “I need connection” is different from “You must play my game.”
All feelings are welcome. Not every action is okay.
Classroom adaptation inspired by Marshall Rosenberg’s NVC and CNVC feelings and needs resources.

posters.title: Say what matters
posters.alt: Four illustrated steps for a clear message: notice, feel, need and request, followed by listening and accessible communication options.
text: Notice · Feel · Need · Request.
1. Notice: Describe what happened, not a guessed intention. “When you use that nickname…”
2. Feel: Name a feeling, not a label for the other person. “…I feel embarrassed.”
3. Need: Say what matters to you. “Respect matters to me.”
4. Request: Ask for a clear, doable action. “Please use my name.”
Then listen: “What did you hear me asking?” “Did I understand you?”
Words, writing, pictures and AAC all count.
You can simply say “Stop,” leave, or seek adult help. No perfect sentence is required.
Classroom adaptation of Marshall Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication.

posters.title: One need, many possible ways
posters.alt: Two friends seek connection through different activities; possible plans, listening checks, requests and safety boundaries are shown.
text: We can care about both people’s needs.
The situation: Two friends want to spend time together, but prefer different games. Shared need: connection.
Possible strategies: Take turns choosing. Find a third activity. Plan time together later.
Listen and check: “Are you wanting some choice?” “Would taking turns work?” A guess is not a fact. Let the person tell you.
Requests are not demands. Someone can say no to a proposed activity.
Boundaries still matter. “Stop” means stop. No one owes unwanted touch or participation. If you feel unsafe, move away and get adult help.
Classroom example inspired by NVC needs and strategies.

posters.title: Healthy boundaries
posters.alt: Healthy boundaries infographic: personal limits, asking and respecting consent, boundaries versus control, words to use, and getting help.
text: My limits matter. Yours do too.
Boundaries protect our bodies, personal space, privacy, time and feelings. Different people can have different limits. Those limits can change.
Ask before touching, borrowing, taking a photo or sharing it. A yes must be freely given. Someone can change their mind. No thanks → Okay. Stop when someone says stop.
Boundary: I will step away if the teasing continues. Control: You are not allowed to have other friends. You can explain your limit without deciding someone else’s friendships.
Words you can use: Stop. Please give me space. Do not share my photo. I need help. You may speak, point, use AAC or ask someone to help you communicate.
If you feel unsafe, move to safety and tell a trusted adult. Keep asking for help. You do not need perfect words. It is not your fault if someone ignores your boundary.
